result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.maximum_branching()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find a maximum-weight branching of a directed graph (Edmonds' algorithm). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L56513-L56608){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.maximum_branching(weight_attr=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Maximum branching](/assets/graphs/maximum-branching.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A weighted directed graph on four nodes: A points to B (3) and D (1), and B, C, D form the cycle B→C (5), C→D (4), D→B (6). The heaviest in-edges would close that cycle, so Edmonds' algorithm drops D→B (dashed) and keeps A→B, B→C, and C→D in the accent color, a single tree rooted at A; A→D is faded. The card lists the three edges and their total weight 3 + 5 + 4 = 12." width="100%"} A branching is a directed forest: no cycles, and every node has at most one incoming edge, so each tree hangs from its own root with all edges pointing away from it. The maximum branching is the branching whose edges have the largest possible total weight. Think of every edge `u -> v` as a vote of confidence in "`v` comes from `u`": the maximum branching assigns each node at most one parent so that the total confidence is as high as possible, without ever creating a cycle of parents. Maximum branchings are used for: - reconstructing hierarchies or lineages from pairwise scores (who derived from whom, which document was copied from which, phylogenies and cascades) - dependency parsing in natural language processing, where words choose their heads - the directed counterpart of a maximum spanning forest Only edges with positive weight help, so edges of weight zero or less are never chosen and the branching need not span the graph (use `maximum_spanning_arborescence()` to force a single tree that reaches every node). Self-loops are never chosen. The original graph is not modified. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weight_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the edge attribute holding the weights. If `None` (the default), each edge's weight field is used (`1.0` on an unweighted graph). Edges that lack the attribute, or hold a non-numeric value, count as `1.0`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new directed graph with every node of the original (IDs, labels and attributes kept) and only the branching's edges (weights and attributes copied). ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is undirected or an edge value is NaN. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Edmonds' algorithm (1967) first gives every node its heaviest positive incoming edge. If these choices contain no cycle they form the optimum. Otherwise each cycle $C$ is contracted into a single node, and an edge $(u, v)$ entering $C$ at $v$ gets the adjusted weight $w(u, v) - w(e_v) + \min_{e \in C} w(e)$, where $e_v$ is the cycle edge into $v$ (Karp 1971): choosing it means swapping $e_v$ out of the cycle, instead of the lightest cycle edge. The contracted problem is solved recursively, and each cycle is expanded by dropping either the edge into the node where the solution enters it or, if nothing enters, its lightest edge. This implementation runs in $O(V E)$ time. When several branchings tie, a different one than NetworkX's may be returned, but the total weight is the same. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Three editors each forwarded a story, and the edge weights score how confident we are that one copied from another. The heaviest choice of "source" for each copy forms a cycle, B -> C -> D -> B, which Edmonds' algorithm breaks at its weakest edge: ::: {#9f26db07 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=True, weighted=True) g.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) g.add_edges( [("A", "B", 3.0), ("B", "C", 5.0), ("C", "D", 4.0), ("D", "B", 6.0), ("A", "D", 1.0)] ) branching = g.maximum_branching() branching.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['A->B', 'B->C', 'C->D'] ``` ::: ::: The result is a single tree rooted at A, with total weight 3 + 5 + 4 = 12. Dropping D -> B (6) instead of B's other in-edge would have stranded the whole cycle: ::: {#b1cb8c04 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( sum(branching.get_edge(e).weight for e in branching.get_edge_ids(limit=None)), branching.is_arborescence(), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (12.0, True) ``` ::: ::: Edges with non-positive weights never pay off, so they are left out even when that splits the result into several trees: ::: {#3eed3cd5 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} g2 = ec.Graph(directed=True, weighted=True) g2.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) g2.add_edges([("A", "B", 2.0), ("B", "C", -1.0)]) g2.maximum_branching().get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['A->B'] ``` ::: :::
